displayQuote: If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants

meta.title: Who really said "If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Isaac Newton did write it — in a 1675 letter to Robert Hooke. But the metaphor was already 500 years old: Bernard of Chartres coined it in the 1100s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants'?
meta.ogDescription: Newton wrote these exact words to Robert Hooke in 1675. Yet the image of dwarfs on giants' shoulders goes back to Bernard of Chartres in the 12th century.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Newton wrote it in his own hand in a letter to Robert Hooke dated 5 February 1675 (Old Style; 1676 by modern reckoning). The autograph manuscript survives, so the wording is firmly his — though the metaphor itself was already centuries old when he used it.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Letter from Isaac Newton to Robert Hooke
The metaphor traces to Bernard of Chartres, 12th century

source.excerpt: What Des-Cartes did was a good step. You have added much several ways, & especially in taking the colours of thin plates into philosophical consideration. If I have seen further it is by standing on the sholders of Giants.
trail: The words are Newton’s own: he wrote them in a letter to Robert Hooke dated 5 February 1675, whose text and history are documented in Wikipedia’s sourced entry.
The fuller passage — crediting Descartes and Hooke’s work on thin-plate colours — is reproduced from the manuscript by The Marginalian.
The metaphor long predates Newton: John of Salisbury (1159) attributes it to Bernard of Chartres, with the earliest attestation in William of Conches’s glosses (c. 1123).
source.excerptNote: From Newton’s autograph letter to Hooke; the manuscript spells it “sholders,” normalised in modern quotation to “shoulders.”

author.name: Isaac Newton
author.heading: About Isaac Newton
author.bio: Sir Isaac Newton was an English mathematician, physicist and astronomer whose Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687) laid the foundations of classical mechanics and universal gravitation. The famous line comes from his correspondence with rival natural philosopher Robert Hooke during a dispute over the theory of light and colour.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The wording is authentically Newton’s — but the popular belief that he coined the idea is wrong. He was reworking a metaphor that had circulated in European learning for over five hundred years.

items.why: The image of dwarfs seeing farther because they stand on giants’ shoulders is credited to the 12th-century scholar Bernard of Chartres by John of Salisbury in his Metalogicon (1159); the earliest surviving attestation is in William of Conches’s glosses on Priscian, c. 1123, per the documented history.

The line is quoted as pure modesty, but it sits inside a barbed exchange with Robert Hooke — who was of slight build and had a pronounced stoop — leading some writers to read a dig beneath the courtesy, as discussed here.

misattribution.truthLine: Newton really wrote these words in 1675, but he was passing along a medieval commonplace, not minting an original thought — see the sourced record.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sentence has become the motto of cumulative science — the acknowledgement that every discovery rests on the work of predecessors. It is engraved on the edge of the British two-pound coin and adorns the title page of countless dissertations.

The irony is that the phrase itself proves its own point: Newton saw further into the metaphor because he was standing on Bernard of Chartres, John of Salisbury and centuries of scribes who kept the image alive.
context.pull: The phrase proves its own point: Newton borrowed it from giants who came before.
